comments.text:
PLEASE READ, IMPORTANT 7900XT(X) INFO! 

You only reviewed 7900XT cards with two 8-pin connectors. I want to chime in here. 

I just bought an ASRock 7900XT Taichi and I realized something that never seems to get attention in reviews: Not all 7900XT and XTX cards are created equal! Not even close.

The models with two 8-pin connectors tend to have weaker coolers and a power limit of around ~350 watts (after applying +15% in Adrenalin).

The models with three 8-pin connectors can draw a little over 400 watts (after +15%) and have the same cooler as the XTX card, aka overkill. My 7900XT has a 70c hotspot temp under full 400 watt load with the fans at 50%.

With an overclock like that, my 7900XT outperforms a base XTX! I get over 30k in Timespy and roughly the same or better FPS in games than 7900XTX cards with two connectors.

It's cool and quiet too, and the Taichi in particular was only $30 more than the cheapeat available 7900XT model.

Yes it draws 400 watts but even at European electricity prices you're still only looking at saving €25/year compared to a 4070Ti if you game 6 hours a day every day. Less in North America. That's a cost you won't notice, let's be honest. The only thing you notice us heat output which I admit is horrible during the summer, but allows me to turn off the heating during the winter lol.

Ampere also consumed heaps of power, nobody cared about AMD being more efficient, somehow with the 4000 series it does matter. Weird.

Also 20GB VRAM is a big deal. Just look at the system specs of new/upcoming Unreal Engine 5 games where 12GB is only goid for 1440P Medium settings, no RT, and Quality upscaling enabled so it actually renders at 960P.

That 20GB VRAM buffer and the three connector model with an XTX cooler (not just the Taichi, other AiBs also sell 7900XT models with three connectors and the XTX cooler) performance blows the 4070Ti out of the water. RT performance of my card is almost the same as a 4070Ti too. 

Above 400 watts, RDNA3 performance scaling is terrible so unless you need the VRAM for productivity or game at native 4K, a 7900XT with three connectors and an XTX cooler for $775  is better value than a basic two connector 7900XTX for $950 imo.

comments.text:
To say someone is mad to still want a 4070 or 4070 ti isn't a particularly level headed assessment. 

It really depends on what the consumer wants to prioritize. The 7900xt is faster at rasterizing and has more vram, but that's about it. The nvidia cards are more efficient, handle heavy RT much better, and FG is nice for heavy RT titles like Cyberpunk and Hogwarts. It's also more useful for non gaming creative workloads. 

I know we can't bench with features on because it's not apples to apples, nonetheless the lack of these features is adding up vs AMD gpus to where Nvidia does what it's doing to market pricing. 

Just as example at 3440x1440 and highlighting the weaknesses of both cards. A 4070ti on can play hogwarts on ultra with ultra RT comfortably around 60fps with dlss or fsr quality. One can then lower textures to high to enable FG at minimal visual penalty but now have over 100fps in this cpu limited singpoe player title. A 7900 xt can outperform the 4070ti when RT is reduced to medium or lower, no FG enabked and it has enough vram to set everything else on ultra without out managing vram capacity. However ultimately, RT is only really impactful at ultra settings from my experience and FG boosts frame rates despite CPU limitaions. Despite the 12gb vram, the 4070ti does provide the superior exprience thanks to those features. Yea RT is useless but mostly in games with limited RT. It is more impactful in RT heavy titles like CP and HL. 

Also, for competitve gameplay online one might want reflex enabled without FG at low grapbics settings that don't saturate vram, vs having 20Gb? Also with so much rasterized performance at this level of GPU, it really is just the vram capacity that makes AMD's card appealing at these price points. (And vram capacity is certainly very helpful)

I just want to say that it is  very easy to make many valid counter arguments to Steve's conclusion. Far too easy to call an nvidia consumer mad to prioritize these features.

comments.text:
I think the real failure on pricing with the latest generations is the phrase, "But you are leaving money on the table".  The crypto-boom created a consumer price anomaly that would easily leave both Nvidia and AMD's financial side scratching their heads.  The jacked up prices due to demand from cryptominers buying up the previous generation gave a false sense to the profit managers that their cards were underpriced in comparison to consumer demand.  That money they left out from the MSRP was picked up by retailers and scalpers, and it would be easy for Nvidia and AMD's profiteers to whine about a poor business decision in regards to untapped price gouging material.  These guys don't want "their investors to be cheated again" this generation.

I also figure another factor in the pricing problem is competition inside the manufacturing of computer components needed for these GPUs.  Nvidia's GPUs are strictly using Micron's GDDR6X memory chips, meaning Nvidia has to concede to Micron's prices.  When it comes to producing the dies, how many competing chip fabricators can provide the latest tech to make the highest performing processors and components possible?  When 1 fabricator holds a monopoly of the best performance fabrication process, that fabricator holds the power to demand the price Nvidia and AMD must pay.  The only way for Nvidia and AMD to really fight back is to literally show there is no demand for their products at such ludicrous prices.  This is literally a war, and people are literally being hurt over it.  The winners are the ones who have less dependency of the other, able to "suffer" not obtaining what they can't reach.

My opinion of the current market, AMD needs to resurrect Crossfire and bring back driver-based mGPU.  A basic rule they need to follow on a new mGPU method, no AFR.  There is a way to make multi-GPU flawless without baking the features directly into the game engines.  I feel the main reason why multi-GPU development was abandoned was not the performance problems but the fact that someone could buy 2 RTX 3070s for $1,000 MSRP or $1,200 (3070ti) and match up with the RTX 3090 with an MSRP of $1,500.  MultiGPU would wreck the flagship GPU sales.  I am very certain there are users out here that would be willing to assist AMD in purchasing dual GPU systems to try out driver-based mGPU.  It would help with the excess stock.

Good insight. I remember the conclusion on your previous 7900 XT review, but I think you are absolutely right about where they should have priced this thing day 1. 

When I saw the Powercolor Hellhound go on sale at MicroCenter for $699, bought it immediately and picked it up the next day. Absolute max frame rates from the Pulse are slightly below what I could get from the HellHound, but I get no stutters, no noise and no lag, although the idle power with two monitors connected is still over 80 watts. I don't know if it was the drivers or just a poor copy of the HellHound, but the Pulse is a much better experience.

Fun Fact:  90% of RX 7900xt after-market models are basically RX 7900xtx.. so be warned..
For example.. Saphire Pulse 7900xt perform well with low noise & temps.. but 7900xtx Saphire Pulse are ok-ish?
Why?.. simple.. 7900xt Saphire Pulse use 300w, while 7900xtx have 355w, but they both have same heatsink specs
So, what the best solution?
Saphire Pulse is not great to start with, because it's only have 6 heat-pipes... it's works well for 7900xt, but meh for 7900xtx
In the other hand.. Powercolor Hellhound already have bigger heatsink with 8 heat-pipes (15% better temps)
So, Saphire Pulse 7900xt works well, but for 7900xtx pick the Powercolor Hellhound model.. also much quiet fans

7900xtx Powercolor Hellhound only reach 61c at 100% usage.. while Saphire Pulse reaches 66c at 100% usage

Personally, I prefer Saphire products, but they mostly focus on their top tier (Nitro+) while going ok-ish for basic models
In the other hand.. Powercolor always go for extra cooling solutions even on basic models.. which is a bonus

XFX Merc 310 is better than Saphire Pulse in terms of cooling for 7900xt/xtx.. but they super large & have very loud fans

Gigabyte / MSI / Asus.. are all not your best friend when it comes to AMD cards..
They perform well.. but they're mostly more expensive with oudated designa (they focus more on Nvidia)

For AMD.. Pick Saphire / Powercolor / XFX.. theeir products always works better with AMD

comments.text:
Not having a working crystal ball makes when to buy an item for the optimum price chancy.  As far as "value" goes, reviewers can give consumers product comparisons, but it really hinges on a particular consumers budget and usecase.  I play RPG games, Guild Wars 2 for the last 3 years, all the Elder Scrolls releases, and prior to GW2, WoW for 12 years (and never returning to a monthly sub).  As for budget, I'm retired and could have bought a 4090, but $1600+ is obscene.  My EVGA 1080Ti ran GW2 on my Hisense 4k 55U8G just fine with sane "pretty" settings.  A cousin went from 1080P to 4K with his X-99 PC with an AMD ref 6900XT.  I looked at Vram, $$$ and performance and bought a PowerColor 7900XTX for $999.99.  No buyers remorse, but upgrading "pretty" gets expensive fast.  
My conclusion?  If your 1080Ti or 2080Ti still works, $600+ for more "pretty" is a steep ask for most.  And do NOT buy a new ($500+) GPU with less than 16G of Vram.  If you can score a 12g GPU or used 1080Ti or 2080Ti for under $200, a worthy budget option.  8gig (currently the $300-500+ price point) or less will just lead to heartbreak and a messy divorce.  PS:  my grandkids get all my PC hand me downs, so they really like it when I buy new stuff.

comments.text:
After finally getting a 3080 10G card from EVGA after being in their queue for what seemed like years (it was), I was happy, although ignorant of the VRAM limitations at the time. After much thought, watching as many videos as possible on comparisons, and remarkable self-restraint, I started seriously considering an AMD based card over an NVIDIA. The only time in my PC gaming years that I've purchased an AMD based card was in the early 2000's, when I bought an ATI card at a local Best Buy, which I returned for an Nvidia based card due to driver issues with running Blade of Darkness. So, last week I saw that AMD was including Starfield with the purchase of certain CPU's and GPU's, and that at my local Micro Center they had the Powercolor 7900 XT Hellhound on sale with Starfield for $699 USD... self-restraint be damned! I ended up upgrading my CPU from a 12600K to a 13700K (swap out on my existing LGA 1700 based board), from the RTX 3080 - 10G to the RX 7900 XT - 20G card, and added a DeepCool LT720 cooler for the CPU, with a copy of the premium version of Starfield for slightly more than the cost of an RTX 4080. 

I've had no issues with Adrenaline, in truth I prefer it over Nvidia Experience (bleh), have a considerable uplift across the board for gaming at 1440p on my current monitor, and with the extra cushion of 20G of VRAM, I feel better knowing I won't have problems due to lack of it, at least for a while. Thank you guys so much for what you do, I appreciate your candor and your wealth of expertise and content you put out regularly, it really helps consumers like myself.

comments.text: Would love to see tier-based cost per frame charts, in which only cards within the same “tier” as the card being reviewed are shown. Comparing “cost per frame” of budget cards to high end cards is not really useful. People don’t buy cards based on “best value” in an absolute sense—they care about value, yes, but only when it comes to selecting between comparable products. That is, they decide a tier of performance that they want, and then within that their they may want to know which is the available options is better value. But knowing that there is some better value product in a lower tier is not that useful. It’s like telling someone looking for a new sports car that they can get a cheap compact car for better “cost-per-horsepower”—that would be irrelevant information.

The difference between 12GB and 16GB is probably more important than the difference between 16GB and 20GB at this performance tier, but more Vram is obviously still better. There are definitely not that many games yet where having more than 12GB is important at 1440p, but I do believe there are some games where this already does make a difference. At 4k, 12GB is definitely not enough for some games, but very few games which would run well at 4k on a 7900 XT or 4070 ti would need more than 12GB. 

That being said, I do believe that 12GB is going to hold back the potential of the RTX 4070 and 4070 ti. If nothing else, the 4070 ti is just way too expensive for a card with only 12GB of Vram in 2023. The 8GB RX 480 was released SEVEN years ago for 240 USD (about 330 USD in today's money, if you adjust for inflation). GDDR6 Memory costs Nvidia and AMD less than FOUR dollars per gigabyte, and the cost of increasing the bus width to accomodate 16GB with a decent bandwidth would also have not cost very much extra at all, and would have significantly increased the bandwidth, and at least somewhat increased overall performance as well, which would have either allowed them to charge more, or would have resulted in them being more popular. 600 and 800 dollar cards should DEFINITELY have more than 12GB in 2023. I have already seen some game developers stating in interviews that 12GB is going to be very limiting at these performance and price tiers, and that 16GB should be considered the MINIMUM for 500+ dollar cards.

comments.text:
@earllemongrab7960  I agree. It would also be nice to have the 6800 XT in there, as it's probably the most common high-end AMD card from last generation, and also currently a better value than the 6950 XT, as it is much closer in performance to a 6950 XT than it is to the 6800, and can be found for about 500-520 USD. 

A used 3090 or used 3090 ti is probably the most competitive alternative to a 7900 XT other than the 7900 XTX, so that definitely makes a lot of sense to include one of them. It could also help to show which games the 12GB of Vram on the 4070 ti or 4070 is a limiting factor, and could also help to show where the 192-bit memory bus is a limiting factor for the 4070 or 4070 ti, though I think the memory bandwidth on those cards is definitely not nearly as big of an issue as their memory capacity. 

The 3090 and 3090 ti were both obviously a poor value when originally released (for most people) but they ARE both very well rounded graphics cards, with no shortage of Vram or memory bandwidth to go with their GPU compute power, unlike the 3080, 3080 ti, 4070, and (especially) the 4070 ti. Some people who bought the 4070 ti seemed to think that it was good because it was so much cheaper than the 3090 and 3090 ti, with similar performance, but if those are the only cards the 4070 ti offers better value than, it's really not saying much, and is not at all the comparison you should be making to justify your purchase. Furthermore, having double the Vram and significantly better memory bandwidth still makes both the 3090 and 3090 ti significantly better products than the 4070 ti, ultimately. There are going to be a lot of games where that superior memory capacity will allow a 3090 or 3090 ti to pull way ahead of a 4070 ti, or simply just allow you to have better textures, or other higher quality settings, without the frame-rate falling off a cliff. 

That being said, they are still extremely power hungry, and I'd be a little afraid to buy one used, especially given that a lot of 3090's seem to have issues with memory failures, likely caused by a combination of weak memory cooling on the back of the card on some models, along with being used in inadequately ventilated cases. It is always nice to have warranty coverage, especially when spending 700+ dollars on a graphics card. If you're lucky, you can find a used 3090 or 3090 ti which is covered by a transferable warranty, but it can be hard to know for sure if a card has a valid warranty or not, because the brands which offered them did still sell some versions which didn't come with that warranty, and the warranty could still potentially be  considered voided by prior improper maintenance or repair work.

@keldon1137  That's definitely not something that either of them has said. Tim and Steve have said that 12GB is probably going to be fine, FOR THE MOST PART, for the 4070 and 4070 ti, but that 16GB would definitely be better at that performance tier, and they have also argued that the 12GB of Vram is particularly bad for a card that's as expensive as the 4070 ti. You have a very selective memory, maybe your brain ran out of Vram. The only thing which might make those cards obsolete in three years is the fact that they only have 12GB of Vram, but you're suggesting that 12GB is enough because they'll be obsolete "in a few years"?!

Good cards from seven years ago, such as the GTX 1060 6GB, RX 480 8GB, GTX 1070, and GTX 1070 ti are still very usable in most games today, with the right settings. Two or three years isn't even that long, but cards with more Vram inevitably age better than ones with similar GPU compute performance but less Vram.

I have seen interviews with two different game developers who have stated that 12GB of Vram is going to be a limiting factor in a lot of games over the next two years, especially for graphics cards in the 500+ dollar price range, where you would expect to be able to run at 1440p, minimum, with good quality settings, for at least a few years. 

Vram currently costs AMD and Nvidia less than 4 dollars per GB. The first mainstream 8GB graphics card was released NINE YEARS AGO for 330 USD. The 8GB RX 480 was released SEVEN years ago for 230 USD, and the 1070 (also with 8GB) was released for 380 USD in the same year. Sure, there's been inflation since then, but only about 20%,  and that's not nearly enough to justify charging 600 for a 12GB card SEVEN YEARS LATER (in 2023), let alone 800. The 12GB of Vram on the 4070 and 4070 ti isn't going to make them completely un-usable over the next few years, but it will significantly limit what graphics settings you will be able to use in some games, and it will also affect texture quality in some games, regardless of what settings you select.

Most graphically demanding games are designed primarily for the consoles, and secondarily for the PC. The latest consoles are massively more powerful than the previous generation ones, especially in terms of memory capacity and SSD/ I/O speed, but also in terms of GPU power, and that's sparked an absolutely massive shift in the way games are made, and that's why we're suddenly seeing games with MASSIVELY higher performance and Vram requirements. It's not because game developers are lazy and bad at optimizing things, though optimization issues are real, and it's always nicer when games are well optimized, but optimization for multiple hardware configurations on PC ports is not nearly as easy or feasible as a lot of people seem to think it is. Nvidia has done such a great job of marketing, that people like you would rather believe that there's something wrong with the game than to believe that Nvidia short-changed you on your Vram capacity, and you're doing free marketing for them, trying to convince others that the 12GB of Vram on the 4070 and 4070 ti are enough. Those two cards would have been much more favourably reviewed if they had both been designed with 16GB of Vram, especially the 4070. 

Nvidia's gaming division is more profitable than AMD's Radeon division precisely because they are better at convincing people to pay more for less. They make a lot of great products, but their products come with a premium, especially lately.

While, on the other hand, what you are saying about VRAM is solely a guess/prediction. Nobody can say for sure, whether 12GB will be enough for 4070 Ti in future games or not. These days I see no need in those 16GB (let alone 20GB) of VRAM for this GPU tier. I mean, it is good to have more, but right now, I would definitely choose features over VRAM. I want to play games now and get the best balance between visual quality and performance. 4070 Ti is the GPU that can provide me such an experience. Those people, who buy 7900 XT are hoping for the future, when AMD drivers get better and increase gaming performance, when AMD will improve FSR and release their own frame gen tech, when 20GB of VRAM will become relevant for gaming. But when this "future" will become? In 2 years, 3 years, 5 years? Nobody knows for sure. In 3 years there will be a new gen of GPUs, which might offer much more than the current one. Are you sure in 2026 you will still be holding on to the GPU you bought in 2023? I am not sure. So why should I bother about potential problems with VRAM (if they will ever happen)?
